text.story:
The door bangs.
Pip drops his bag.
“Everyone is annoying.”

Dee stops beside the table. Pip pushes his bag under it with his foot, but the strap catches. He kicks again. The bag stays put.

“I don't want questions.”

“Something about this afternoon feels hard,” Dee says. “You don't have to tell the whole thing right now.”

Pip pulls the strap free. He sits, then stands again. Sitting feels wrong. Standing feels wrong too.

Dee stays beside the other chair without reaching for his bag.

“I said everyone,” Pip says.

“I heard you.”

On the table lies a comic page with an empty speech bubble. A pencil rests across the bubble like a tiny microphone. Pip nudges it with one finger.

“Even my speech bubble wants a turn,” he mutters.

Dee looks at the pencil. “It has a very small microphone.”

Pip almost smiles. Almost. Then he pushes the page away.

“I'm still mad.”

“Okay,” Dee says. “Want to find the word that fits, or leave that for later?”

“Mad fits.”

“It might.”

Pip presses his palms against the table. “What if I don't know?”

“You can try a word without keeping it.”

He watches the pencil roll into the fold of the paper. The afternoon sits in his head like a crowded comic panel, but he doesn't want to describe any of it.

“Can you show me once?”

Dee pulls out the other chair and sits.

“Think of one small thing that bugged you this week. Say the first word that comes. Probably bad, or mad. Now find a sharper word. Annoyed? Embarrassed? Left out? Let down? Jealous? Nervous? Pick one. If two fit, say both. Say it out loud: 'I felt embarrassed, and a bit annoyed.' Now give it a number from 1 to 10. That's it. The word is a tool, not a grade.”

Pip rubs the edge of the table.

“That's a lot of words.”

“You only need the one that fits. Or two.”

“Does saying it fix anything?”

Dee shakes her head. “In adult studies, naming feelings helped people feel less upset. We need stronger tests with children aged 8 to 13.”

Pip looks down at his hands. He doesn't feel much different from a minute ago.

“Annoyed,” he says, then wrinkles his nose. “No. Bigger than annoyed.”

Dee waits.

“Frustrated. Like everything is getting in my way, and I can't get past it.”

He hooks his foot around the chair leg and finally sits.

“Frustrated fits better than bad.”

“That sounds more precise,” Dee says. “Closer to what you mean.”

Pip touches his chest. Dee touches hers too.

“Frustrated,” he says aloud.

“I'm concerned,” Dee says. “I care about how you're doing, and I don't know much about this afternoon.”

Pip slides the comic page back toward himself. He leaves its speech bubble empty.

“Mine's a seven,” he says. “Not a grade. Just how big.”

Dee nods.

“There's another one,” Pip says. “Nervous. Tryouts are next week. They keep popping into my head.”

His fingers tighten around the pencil. He puts it down again.

“Still frustrated. A bit nervous too.”

“You found words for both,” Dee says.

“I didn't tell you what happened.”

“I know.”

“And I'm not ready.”

Dee stays in her chair. Pip stays in his. The bag strap still sticks out beneath the table, and he moves his foot around it instead of kicking.

After a while, Dee asks, “What was the move?”

Pip touches his chest again. “Name what I feel. Frustrated and nervous.”

He glances at the door. Tomorrow's school afternoon still feels too close. But this time, when Dee looks at him, he has two words he can say.
